newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU further probes French textiles aid plan.
newsitem.headline: EU further probes French textiles aid plan.

text.p: The European Commission said on Wednesday it had asked France for more information about measures to help its textile industry which are being closely watched by German and Italian rivals.

The Commission openly questioned in May a 2.1-billion-franc ($408 million) proposal to reduce salary-linked social security contributions paid by textile, clothing and leather industries in France to stimulate job creation.
While encouraging measures to boost employment, the Commission warned at the time that the French plan could distort competition in the European Union's market.

France counter-attacked by saying the help was necessary to compensate for collective agreements in the sectors concerned on the reduction of working hours which resulted in increased costs for the companies.
It also said the measures would have little impact on competition, especially when large companies were concerned because they were the least affected by the agreements.

In May, while approving the scheme for small companies -- in so far that state support was not above 100,000 European currency units per firm over a three-year period -- the Commission said it had objections about some 1,300 larger firms being part of the scheme. Large firms were described as employing more than 50 people.
In Wednesday's statement it re-stated its fears about unfair competition and objected to the French state covering costs resulting from union-management deals.

"The Commission normally believes that costs resulting from agreements between social partners in a given sector -- whether they concern flexible working hours or other aspects which translate in salary increases or paid leave -- must be financed by the companies themselves", it said in the statement.

The Commission has consistently rejected other national attempts in the recent past to help specific industries resist international competition. It particularly outlawed similar measures for the Italian shoe industry and Belgian export-led firms.

Commission sources said that German textile industry unions were also putting the pressure on Bonn to benefit from the same measures as their French rivals if allowed by the Commission. Italian companies were also carefully watching that France did not get away with something that was refused to them.

Rather than sectoral aid measures -- which are seen as distorting competition in the EU's single market -- the Commission encourages general, across the board, reduction of contributions to social security schemes as a way to reduce the bloc's huge unemployment. ($ = 5.150 French Francs)
